arxiv-2606-05169: A benchmark tests only a slice of what a language model can do, the way a 2D slice reveals only part of a 3D object. arxiv-2606-05469: At the Large Hadron Collider, near-miss collisions of lead nuclei flood the detectors with photons that can birth charm quarks. arxiv-2606-05769: Predicting what happens next in a video is easier if you first imagine it. arxiv-2606-06169: Phase-field models simulate cracks growing through materials — but real materials break by their own strength criteria. arxiv-2606-06369: Scene graphs — structured descriptions of images — improve when the model knows visual commonsense. arxiv-2606-06669: Sidon sets — numbers with all-distinct pairwise sums — can sometimes be decomposed into simpler pieces. This paper tackles the Sidon decomposition problem in abelian groups of bounded torsion. The decomposition reveals hidden structure in these extremal sets of integers.
arxiv-2606-06469: Machine learning loves interpolators — models that fit training data exactly. But how abundant are good ones? This paper asks how many interpolating functions actually generalize well. The answer reshapes how we think about overfitting. Not all interpolators are created equal.
arxiv-2606-06769: Testing hypotheses sequentially — as data arrives — with constraints is statistically delicate. This paper develops sequential testing for conditionally constrained hypotheses. arxiv-2606-07169: Posterior predictive checks test Bayesian models — but can they identify the learning rate? This paper answers exactly when, with exact degeneracy results in Gaussian models. The answer clarifies what model checks can reveal. Model checks have limits. The theory clarifies what they reveal.
arxiv-2606-00069: LiDAR segmentation for self-driving needs uncertainty awareness. Invascal self-calibrates with inverse-vacuity for range-view semantic segmentation. The calibration knows when the sensor is unsure. Automotive sensors must know their limits. Proper calibration enables genuinely safe autonomy. Safety cannot ever be compromised.
tob-10469:
Aquinas turns from God to human life in Part I-II of the Summa, the first half of its second part. The subject is how people act and why. Happiness, the will, good and evil in actions, and the passions all come under his question-and-answer method.

Habits receive close attention: how repeated acts become virtues or vices, and what roles law and grace play in making a life good. Aquinas maps the moral life with an engineer's care, defining terms before judging cases. Readers meet the framework behind centuries of Catholic ethics, including ideas about natural law that later reached far beyond the church.
tob-10969:
The complete Douay-Rheims Bible joins the Old Testament translated at Douai in 1609 with the New Testament translated at Rheims in 1582, in Bishop Richard Challoner's eighteenth-century revision. Challoner modernized spelling and softened the most Latin-heavy phrasing, producing the text most later readers know. For three hundred years this was the English Bible of Catholics worldwide.

From Genesis to Revelation, the translation stays formal and Latinate, close to the Vulgate that stood behind it. Psalms and Gospels alike carry the wording generations of Catholics prayed from memory. Traditionalists still favor it, and readers comparing English Bibles will find its differences from the King James Version instructive.
tob-0169:
Joseph Andrew Blackwell's translation presents the Elder Eddas, the old Norse poems associated with Saemund Sigfusson, alongside material from the Younger Edda of Snorri Sturluson. Gods and heroes speak in their own stark verse. Odin's gallows-wisdom in the Hávamál, the seeress's prophecy of Ragnarök, and the lays of Sigurd stand among the highlights.

These poems, preserved in Icelandic manuscripts, are the wellspring of Norse mythology: creation from a giant's body, the world tree, and the gods' foreknown doom at the twilight. Blackwell's version keeps their power in older English dress. Readers who know Norse myth only through retellings will find the originals stranger, funnier, and more fatalistic.
galton-hereditary-genius-1869:
Francis Galton published Hereditary Genius in 1869, his first book on inherited ability. He collected the family histories of judges, statesmen, scientists, and other eminent men. Patterns in those pedigrees drive his whole argument.

Galton claims that talent clusters in families because nature outweighs training. He ranks relatives by closeness and counts how eminence fades with distance. The inquiry launched the nature-versus-nurture debate in modern form. It also launched eugenics, whose harms readers must keep in view. The statistical ambition was real; so were the blind spots. Galton later expanded its methods into the statistical study of human differences generally.
brasseur-manuscrit-troano-vol-1-1869:
One of the few Maya books to survive the conquest came to print in 1869. Manuscrit Troano, volume one, is Brasseur de Bourbourg's first publication of the Troano Codex. The French edition opened the painted manuscript to the scholars of Europe.

Brasseur prints the codex pages and begins his study of Maya script and tongue. He read the signs as a tale of land lost to the sea, a reading few now accept. From his misreading, Le Plongeon later drew the name Mu for a sunken land. The volume still marks the birth of Troano study.
bolender-draft-1969:
Blue Book shut in 1969, but the Air Force still had to field UFO reports that touched national safety. The Bolender Draft, a memo of October 20, 1969, from General Carroll Bolender, lays out how. It tells which reports should still move up a sealed chain.

Bolender writes that reports which bear on the safety of the nation are not part of the Blue Book system. They were to be handled by other Air Force paths once the public program died. The draft shows the quiet afterlife of the UFO desk. It has fed years of debate on what the service kept back.
blue-book-termination-1969:
The Air Force signed the death warrant of its UFO study on December 17, 1969. News Release 1077-69, from Secretary Robert Seamans, tells the world Project Blue Book is done. Twenty years of files, sightings, and public mail end with this one plain sheet.

The release holds that the study could not be backed on grounds of national safety or of science. No case in the files, it says, shows craft past the skill of earth. The words are dry and flat, and the effect was vast. Blue Book's end is the hinge of the whole government UFO tale.
catoe-ufo-bibliography-1969:
Lynn Catoe of the Library of Congress mapped the whole UFO shelf in 1969. UFOs and Related Subjects is her annotated bibliography, made for the Air Force Office of Scientific Research. The book runs to 417 pages of entries and notes.

Books, reports, and magazine work stand in neat ranks, each with a fair word on its worth. Catoe wastes no awe and no scorn; her tone is that of a guide, not a judge. The volume shows how vast the UFO field had grown by the end of Blue Book. It stays the standard map of that field.
randolph-pre-adamite-man-1869:
Paschal Beverly Randolph claimed man is far more old than the Good Book says in Pre-Adamite Man, out in 1869. Bands of men, he held, lived and built on earth long ere Adam. He draws on stone tools, old bones, and tales from the East to make his bold case for deep time.

The claim was hot stuff in his day. Church men balked, while men of the dig cheered parts of it. Randolph gives the claim an occult spin all his own. The book is his word in a great row of his age. Stone finds in his day had just begun to shake old views. Randolph seized on them fast to back his claim of man's deep age.
randolph-love-and-its-hidden-history-186:
Paschal Beverly Randolph wrote of love as a force of fate in Love and Its Hidden History, out in 1869. He held that love binds souls by laws as strict as those of the stars. A wrong bond can blight a life. A right one can lift both souls to health and sight.

Rules, tales, and warns fill the book. It is the hands-on mate to his later Eulis! Fans who sought his lore in full read the pair as one. The book shows his warm, grave voice at its best. Randolph wed twice and knew love's joys and griefs at first hand. That past gives his grave rules a warmth texts of law lack.
sargent-planchette-1869:
Epes Sargent took up arms for the faith in Planchette, his book of 1869. Its flip name calls science to scorn: The Despair of Science. The planchette was a small board on wheels that spelled words in the dark room. Sargent, a news man, holds that its words mock the cold creed that all is mere stuff and force.

He prints cases, talks with the dead, and sharp words for his foes. His aim is to show the lab has no key for these doors. The book is the faith's best fight back of its age in his land.
dunraven-experiences-spiritualism-home-1:
Lord Adare kept a log of dark nights in Experiences in Spiritualism with Mr. D. D. Home, out in 1869. Adare, heir to an earl, sat with Home through 1867 to 1869. He writes each night's feats as they came: sounds, moves, forms, and a famed float past the panes of a high room in London town.

His rank and calm tone gave the tales great weight. The log was meant for a small ring, yet soon roamed wide. It is the best guest's eye tale of the top seer at work. Doubt it or not, it grips.
arnold-culture-anarchy-1869:
Matthew Arnold published Culture and Anarchy in 1869, a set of essays on English society. Arnold defines culture as the pursuit of perfection through knowledge of the best that has been thought and said. Against culture he sets anarchy: each person doing as he likes without shared standards. He sorts England into Barbarians, Philistines, and Populace by class.

Sweetness and light is his shorthand for beauty and intelligence joined. The book became the founding text of modern cultural criticism in English. Arnold's urbane wit softens a serious call for public standards. Debates about culture and education still start from his terms. It is his most famous prose work.
mill-subjection-women-1869:
John Stuart Mill published The Subjection of Women in 1869, a founding text of liberal feminism. Mill argues that the legal subordination of women is wrong in itself and bad for society. What is called women's nature, he says, is an artificial product of forced repression. No one can know women's capacities until they are free.

He demands equal education, equal access to work, and the vote. The argument proceeds from utility and justice together. Mill credited many ideas to his wife, Harriet Taylor Mill. The book scandalized many Victorian readers. It remains a model of clear, principled argument for equality.
lecky-european-morals-1869:
W. E. H. Lecky published History of European Morals in 1869, a classic Victorian study of moral ideas. Lecky traces how standards of right and wrong changed from the Roman Empire to his own century. He treats slavery, charity, chastity, and the treatment of animals and enemies. Pagan and Christian morals are weighed in turn.

Lecky writes with calm learning and wide reading in primary sources. He credits Christianity with raising charity, yet faults its record on tolerance and the intellect. The book became the standard history of morals for generations. Its method shaped later work on the history of ideas. It remains clear, fair, and absorbing.
wallace-malay-archipelago-1869:
Alfred Russel Wallace spent eight years in the islands of Malaysia and Indonesia collecting birds, insects, and mammals. His 1869 book The Malay Archipelago tells that journey in full. He supported himself by selling specimens to museums and collectors back home. He wrote it after he and Darwin had jointly announced natural selection.

Wallace describes volcanoes, jungles, rare birds of paradise, and the peoples who guided and fed him. He also notes a sharp line dividing the islands' animal life, still called Wallace's Line by scientists. The narrative mixes danger, illness, and wonder with calm, exact observation. The book remains a founding story of biogeography, the study of where species live and why.
finney-character-claims-of-freemasonry-1:
Charles G Finney, a leading revival preacher, published his attack on Freemasonry in 1869. Finney said he had once been a Mason himself, and he wrote as a Christian minister alarmed by the lodge. His target was not one lodge but the whole system.

Finney examined Masonic oaths, claims, and daily practice, and argued that they conflicted with Christian faith and honest public life. He warned that secret pledges could place a brother Mason above church, family, or court. The book became a key text for evangelical critics, and it shows how sharp the clash between revival faith and lodge loyalty could be.
beguin-tyrocinium-chymicum-1669:
Jean Béguin's Tyrocinium Chymicum, first issued in Latin in 1610, appeared in English in 1669. Béguin taught chemistry in Paris and wrote for beginners, as his title's word for a first lesson suggests. His primer was among the first clear textbooks of the new chemical art.

Lessons define terms, describe vessels and furnaces, and give recipes for medicines from plants, animals, and minerals. Béguin favored plain steps over the riddles of older alchemical writers. Students across Europe learned from the book for decades. It shows chemistry stepping away from secret symbols toward teaching that any trained reader could follow and repeat.
macoy-general-history-freemasonry-1869:
Robert Macoy published his General History, Cyclopedia and Dictionary of Freemasonry in 1869 in New York. Macoy was a major American Masonic publisher and organizer. He meant the volume as a single reference work that a lodge member or curious reader could keep at hand.

Entries cover symbols, degrees, officers, and terms, while longer sections trace the order from early guilds to modern lodges. Biographies of noted Masons and accounts of rites in many lands fill out the survey. Macoy wrote as a supporter of the craft, not a critic. The book remains a handy record of how American Masonry described itself in the nineteenth century.
agrippa-vanitie-and-uncertaintie-1569:
Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa's attack on the arts and sciences appeared in English in 1569, translated by James Sandford. The Latin original, De Vanitate, had shocked readers decades earlier. Agrippa, himself a famed scholar and occult writer, turned on the very learning he practiced.

Chapter by chapter, Agrippa mocked the claims of grammar, poetry, history, medicine, law, theology, and magic itself. He showed experts disagreeing, frauds thriving, and each art failing to give sure truth. Only faith, he argued, stood firm. The book is a great skeptical performance, half serious and half sly. It influenced later doubters and shows how deep distrust of experts ran even at the height of Renaissance learning.
wallace-malay-archipelago-vol-1-1869:
Alfred Russel Wallace published Volume 1 of The Malay Archipelago in 1869, after eight years of travel in the islands between Asia and Australia. Wallace earned his living by collecting specimens for sale. At the same time he formed, on his own, the theory of natural selection that Charles Darwin also reached.

Volume 1 follows Wallace through Singapore, Malaya, and the great islands of the west, describing forests, volcanoes, and peoples. He logged birds, insects, and mammals, and noted sharp changes in species from island to island. Those changes led to the line now called the Wallace Line. The book mixes adventure, sharp observation, and science of the first rank.
wallace-malay-archipelago-vol-2-1869:
Volume 2 of Wallace's Malay Archipelago appeared in 1869, completing his account of eight years in the islands of Southeast Asia and New Guinea. Alfred Russel Wallace had collected more than a hundred thousand specimens on the trip. The second volume moves east, toward the lands of birds of paradise.

Wallace described the Aru Islands, New Guinea, and the Moluccas, with their rare birds and distinct peoples. He compared island species on each side of a deep divide now called the Wallace Line. His notes on the bird of paradise hunts remain famous. The volume closes a travel book that is also a founding work of the study of how species are spread across the earth.
browning-ring-and-book-vol1-1869:
Robert Browning built his longest poem on a real Roman murder case from the 1690s. He found the trial records in an old book bought in Florence. The Ring and the Book came out in four volumes in 1868 and 1869, and this is the first.

The opening book explains how Browning found the records and shaped his plan. Then the voices begin: Roman gossips, the murdered woman's family, and others each tell the story their own way. A count has killed his young wife, and every witness sees the crime differently. The method lets truth emerge slowly from clashing accounts.
browning-ring-and-book-vol2-1869:
Robert Browning's long poem The Ring and the Book retells a Roman murder trial from the 1690s. He published it in four volumes across 1868 and 1869. This second volume holds Books Five through Eight of the twelve-book poem.

Each book gives the same crime to a new speaker. Here the lawyers argue, the accused count defends himself, and other voices weigh in with gossip and guesswork. No two accounts agree, and Browning trusts the reader to sort truth from self-interest. The middle volumes show his method at full stretch, turning dry court papers into living drama.
browning-ring-and-book-vol3-1869:
Robert Browning shaped The Ring and the Book from real records of a murder trial held in Rome in 1698. The poem came out in four volumes in 1868 and 1869. This third volume holds Books Nine through Eleven.

These books carry the longest and most moving speeches in the whole poem. The murdered wife, Pompilia, tells her story on her deathbed, and the priest Caponsacchi describes his attempt to rescue her. The Pope himself then weighs the case in a famous reflective speech. Together they build steadily toward the verdict that the final volume delivers at last.
browning-ring-and-book-vol4-1869:
Robert Browning closed his longest poem, The Ring and the Book, with this fourth volume, published in 1869. The poem retells a Roman murder case of 1698 through twelve separate speeches. Book Twelve, held in this volume, ends the whole design.

Browning steps forward in his own voice to judge what the many speakers have shown. He explains the gold-and-alloy image behind his title, the ring made from mixed metal and shaped by craft. Letters and reports after the trial round out the record. The ending defends the poem's method: truth found by testing many partial accounts against each other.
leger-histoire-eglises-vaudoises-1669:
Jean-Paul Léger, a Waldensian pastor, wrote the general history of the evangelical churches of the valleys of Piedmont in 1669. His own people, the Vaudois, had kept their faith in the Alpine valleys since long before the Reformation. The book is in French. Léger wrote as pastor, witness, and exile after the massacres of 1655.

The first book sets out the doctrine and discipline of the valley churches. The second tells the persecutions, rising to the Piedmontese Easter of 1655, when ducal troops slaughtered the Vaudois and Milton's sonnet cried out across Europe. Léger prints the papers and the names. His history is the founding archive of the Waldensian memory.
reid-inquiry-human-mind-1769:
Thomas Reid, a Scottish professor, published An Inquiry into the Human Mind in 1764. The edition of 1769 is the text here, carrying his principles of common sense. Reid wrote against the ideal theory, the view that the mind knows only its own ideas. David Hume had drawn bleak results from that view, and Reid aimed to answer him at the root.

Reid argues that belief in an outer world, and in other minds, rests on common sense built into human nature. Perception, on his account, reaches the world itself, not a screen of images. The Inquiry founded the Scottish common-sense school of philosophy. Its plain, sturdy method still appeals to readers tired of elegant doubt.
morgagni-sedibus-alexander-vol1-1769:
Giovanni Battista Morgagni founded pathological anatomy in De sedibus, first printed in Latin in 1761. Benjamin Alexander translated the work into English in 1769, and volume one begins the set. Morgagni compared the symptoms of the sick with the lesions found after death. His records drew on some seven hundred autopsies.

Letter by letter, he matches bedside stories to damaged organs. That matching created clinicopathological reasoning, still the core of diagnosis. Volume one opens a three volume English set. Doctors learned from it to ask where disease sits in the body. The change in thinking was enormous. Modern pathology starts on these pages.
morgagni-sedibus-alexander-vol2-1769:
Volume two of Alexander's 1769 English Morgagni continues De sedibus, the seats and causes of diseases. The first volume began Morgagni's letters matching symptoms to organ lesions. This volume carries the survey through the middle of his five Latin books. Its last page ends book three, as the original note records.

Autopsy reports pile up, each tying a case history to findings in the body. Chest, belly, and the organs between them receive their share of cases. Morgagni's method stays steady: observe, open, compare, and record. The volume forms the center of a three part set. Pathologists still honor the discipline shown here. It is heavy reading with heavy rewards.
morgagni-sedibus-alexander-vol3-1769:
Alexander's English Morgagni ends with volume three, printed in 1769 like its fellows. The Latin De sedibus of 1761 reshaped medicine by rooting disease in organs. This closing volume finishes the remaining books of cases. A general index ends the set, marked by the words The End.

Morgagni's letters complete their long survey of the body's seats of illness. Symptoms recorded in life stand matched with lesions found in death, case after case. The full English set runs to three volumes. Together they founded pathological anatomy for English readers. Few medical works of the century carried more weight. The index alone shows the scope.
borlase-antiquities-cornwall-1769:
Fifteen years after his first Cornwall volume, William Borlase brought out a second, larger edition in 1769. The Antiquities of Cornwall had grown with its author and with the county lore sent to him. Borlase revised the text, added new material, and folded in his Observations, giving the work its fullest and most settled form.

The same great subjects return: stone circles, cromlechs, and inscribed stones across the county, now more fully drawn. With more sites recorded and earlier claims rethought, the edition stands as the mature shape of his Cornish corpus. Readers who want Borlase at his most complete come to the 1769 printing rather than the first.
grettir-saga-magnusson-morris-1869:
Grettir the Strong killed a ghost, outlived a curse, and held out as an outlaw for nineteen years in Iceland. His saga, translated by Eiríkr Magnússon and William Morris in 1869, tells of strength wasted by temper and fate. Grettir could beat any man or monster, yet could not master his fear of the dark.

Hauntings, wrestling matches with the undead, and lonely winters on a sea-girt rock fill the tale. Morris loved the sagas and helped give them their English shape in versions like this one. The Story of Grettir stands as the greatest of the Icelandic family sagas in outlaw form, grim and human at once.
salmon-conic-sections-1869:
George Salmon, an Irish scholar, wrote his Treatise on Conic Sections as a textbook of analytic geometry. The 1869 edition was the standard Victorian version, used by students for decades. Salmon later became a noted churchman, but math made his name.

The book studies the ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola through algebra. Salmon shows how one set of equations can describe all three curves and their shared traits. Clear proofs and many worked cases made it a model textbook. Generations of students learned the geometry of cones and orbits from Salmon's orderly pages. Salmon treats both the pure curves and their use in the wider geometry course.
plos-pone-0003369:
Jeremy R. Sanford and co-authors published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was SF2/ASF, a protein that helps cut and paste gene messages before use. The protein also moves back and forth between the cell nucleus and the outer cell body. The team set out to list which messages it binds in each place.

Inside, the authors explain how they pulled the protein from cells and read the RNA tied to it. They report separate target lists for the nucleus and for the outer cell body. Those lists link one protein to splicing, message export, and protein building. The work helps explain how a single factor can guide a message from gene to finished protein.
plos-pone-0003469:
Virginia Tirino and co-authors hunted stem-like cells in solid tumors for this 2008 paper. Osteosarcoma is the most common primary tumor of bone. Solid tumors mix many cell types with unlike roles. A small subset may hold stem cell powers and drive growth.

The team detected and characterized cells marked by CD133 in human tumors. Such cells may gain aggressiveness and resist treatment. Killing the root cells could stop tumors from regrowing. This survey helps define what those cancer stem cells look like. Bone tumors strike the young most often, raising the stakes of relapse.
plos-pone-0003569:
Xinjiang Cai and David E. Clapham traced a sperm channel's evolution in this 2008 paper. CatSper channels are calcium channels found only in sperm. They drive the hyperactive swimming sperm need to reach the egg. Four subunits plus an auxiliary part form the channel complex.

Across mammals, the family showed lineage-specific gene loss. It also showed rapid evolution in the lines that kept it. Such restless history is common in reproduction genes. Sperm competition may drive that fast, uneven change. Male fertility has few drug options, so channel biology draws steady interest.
plos-pone-0003669:
Rocio G. Urdinguio, Lidia Lopez-Serra, Pilar Lopez-Nieva, and colleagues published this neurology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Rett syndrome is a severe disorder that mainly affects girls and is tied to faults in the MECP2 gene. Mice that lack Mecp2 are a standard model of the disease.

The team searched these mice for changes in neurons that could serve as new treatment targets. Finding fresh targets matters because no cure yet exists for this disorder. Their results add candidate points where future drugs might act to ease a lifelong condition that takes skills away after early growth.
plos-pone-0003769:
Jialiang Wang, Hui Wang, Zhizhong Li, and colleagues published this brain cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Malignant gliomas are among the most lethal cancers known. Their cells form a hierarchy, with cancer stem cells at the top that can regrow the tumor. The team asked what keeps those stem cells going.

They found the gene c-Myc is required for the maintenance of glioma cancer stem cells. Without Myc's support, the self-renewing core of the tumor falters. The result points to a weak spot in the hierarchy that makes gliomas so hard to kill.
plos-pone-0003869:
Ruchi Jain, Bappaditya Dey, Neeraj Dhar, and colleagues published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The BCG vaccine protects against tuberculosis unevenly, with efficacy from zero to eighty percent against adult disease. Better vaccine candidates are needed. One route is recombinant BCG that overproduces strong antigens of the TB bacterium.

The team built a recombinant BCG expressing the antigen Ag85C. It gave enhanced and enduring protection against tuberculosis in their tests. The stronger protection was associated with a changed cytokine profile in the lung, linking the vaccine's effect to the local immune mix. A stronger first shot could protect more of those at risk.
plos-pone-0003969:
Andrew W. Horne, John A. Phillips, Nicole Kane, and co-authors measured a receptor in ectopic pregnancy in 2008. Ectopic pregnancy happens when an embryo lodges in the Fallopian tube. It is a major cause of illness in early pregnancy. In mice, silencing the CB1 cannabinoid receptor traps embryos in the tube.

Their PLOS ONE article measured CB1 in women's Fallopian tubes and decidua. CB1 levels were lower in samples from ectopic pregnancies. That parallel with mice suggests the same system guards embryo travel in humans. The finding may help predict or prevent tubal pregnancies. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004069:
Thomas Fischer, Falko Nagel, Stefan Jacobs, and co-authors rechecked a cancer receptor measure in 2008. CXCR4 is a chemokine receptor that steers cell migration. It guides cancer cells toward specific sites where they seed metastases. Knowing a tumor's CXCR4 status could predict its course.

Earlier attempts to locate the receptor in tissue proved unreliable. Their PLOS ONE article validates a new rabbit antibody called UMB-2. With it, they reassessed normal and tumor tissues. A trustworthy stain is the first step toward CXCR4-guided therapy choices. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004169:
John Heidelberg and colleagues published this genomics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many bacteria and archaea carry CRISPR arrays, stored snippets of DNA from past invaders, together with cas genes. Together they give the microbes a form of acquired immunity against viruses.

The team read genomic data from two heat-loving Synechococcus microbes living in a microbial mat, a layered community of microbes. By comparing host CRISPR records with viral genomes from the same mat, they traced an arms race in action. The study shows germ warfare at the gene level, with hosts and viruses changing together over time.
plos-pone-0004269:
Patrick Reeves and Christopher Richards published this genetics methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Spotting genetic breaks between populations is key to studies of biodiversity and evolution, and to association genetics. Small genetic breaks can hide inside one named population. The most widely used inference methods are model-based Bayesian tools that can be slow and assumption-heavy.

The authors present an approach based on principal coordinates, a statistical way to summarise genetic distances. They show it can detect subtle population structure and other genetic breaks. A lighter method for spotting fine divisions helps researchers working with large, complex samples.
plos-pone-0004369:
John Castle and colleagues published this metabolism study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Acetyl-CoA carboxylases ACC1 and ACC2 catalyse the conversion of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA, controlling how fats are made and burned. They are potential targets for treating metabolic syndrome. Late April brought the Union flag back over New Orleans, a loss the South felt in every European counting house. Cotton, credit, and sympathy all shifted with such news. Dayton's report from Paris that week belongs to the record of how France absorbed the blow to the Confederate cause it was tempted to aid. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d369: A translated paper dated 31 July 1862 stands as Document 369 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Filed in the French section after the Mercier letters. The heading marks it only as a translation, giving no author or reader. So the entry rests on its date, its form, and its place among the French papers of that summer.
frus-1862-d469:
George Perkins Marsh wrote from Turin to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 4 April 1862. His dispatch is Document 469 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress with the annual message.

Spring 1862 found Italy watching France closely, since French troops still guarded the pope in Rome and French ambition was moving in Mexico. Marsh's reports linked those Italian concerns to the American war, which shared the same French question. From Turin he could also report the new kingdom's steady sympathy for the Union. The letter is part of the volume's Italian file, where diplomacy ran on shared national hopes rather than on fear or bargaining.
frus-1862-d569:
Henry Shelton Sanford sent this report from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 September 1862. It is Document 569 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Sanford wrote four days after Lincoln's emancipation order was issued, though the news was still crossing the Atlantic. His report covered the Brussels scene as it stood: the court's connections, the press, and the war's standing in Belgian opinion. Within days he would have the emancipation news to work with, and few ministers used it more eagerly. The letter catches the Belgian file at the hinge of the autumn. The war's new moral shape had not yet reached Europe. When it did, it changed Sanford's brief for the better.
frus-1862-d669:
On 24 December 1861, Anson Burlingame wrote from China to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Burlingame was the American minister there, a former congressman turned envoy. His letter is document 669 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

A Christmas Eve date on a letter from the far side of the world hints at the pace of the post. Mail from China took months to reach Washington, so envoys wrote often and covered much ground in each sheet. Burlingame's dispatch is part of that steady flow, the raw stuff from which the State Department built its view of China in the war years.
frus-1863p1-d69:
William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 2 February 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 69 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, opening Seward's February mail in the file.

February brought no rest to the London brief. The South's agents still worked for ships and friends in Britain, and the Union's claims still needed pressing. Seward's letters kept Adams supplied with the government's views and the facts from home. This one opens a run of February sheets that runs thick in the volume, proof of how much of the war was fought with pens.
frus-1863p1-d169:
Charles Francis Adams closed a three-letter day with this dispatch of 24 April 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 169 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The last of Adams's three sheets wound up the legation's work for a peak day in the file. His spring letters, read whole, are the story of the Union's cause in Britain told by its keeper. This one ends the 24 April set. It stands in the record as a working piece of the watch that kept Britain's fleet and yards from the South.
frus-1863p1-d269: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 August 1863. It is document 269 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the London correspondence on Britain and the Civil War. Letters on this route carried Adams's reading of British policy while Washington worked to keep Britain from backing the Confederacy.
frus-1863p1-d369:
A formal note dated 26 January 1863 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 369 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

British subjects caught up in the war, as sailors, traders, or prisoners, gave London steady grounds for protest. Seward's notes answered those complaints one case at a time. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d469:
A 20 April 1863 dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d569:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State received a letter dated 17 June 1863 from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d669:
Among the day's business on 19 November 1863 was a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

From the London end, the work was pressure and reporting. Adams pushed the British government on Confederate shipbuilding and sent home his reading of British politics and opinion. Read in sequence, the London letters show how close the two countries came to open conflict, and how both sides kept stepping back. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
plos-pbio-0000069:
Unnur Styrkarsdottir, Jean-Baptiste Cazier, Augustine Kong, and others mapped an osteoporosis risk region in PLOS Biology in 2003. Their search ties weak bones to chromosome 20 and to BMP2, a gene known for helping bone form. Osteoporosis thins bone and raises the risk of breaks in older people.

The team used family data to find where the risk sits in the genome, then narrowed it to a gene that fits the biology. That link matters because bone density runs in families, yet the genes behind it were mostly unknown. Naming a region and a likely gene gives drug and diagnosis work a place to start. It also helps explain why some people lose bone faster than others.
plos-pbio-0020069:
Martin Wu, Ling V. Sun, Jessica Vamathevan, and a big team sequenced a parasite genome for PLOS Biology in 2004. Wolbachia pipientis wMel lives inside fruit fly cells and bends the fly's reproduction to spread itself. Its whole genome runs to about 1.27 million DNA letters.

For a free-living bacterium that genome is small and stripped down. Yet it is packed with mobile DNA elements that copy and move within the genome, an odd trait for so compact a genome. The full sequence lets researchers compare Wolbachia strains and track how it manipulates hosts. That knowledge may aid pest control, since Wolbachia infects many insect species of concern.
plos-pbio-0020369:
Olaf Sporns and Rolf Kötter analyzed patterns in brain wiring in PLOS Biology in 2004. Brain networks can be read as maps of nodes and links. Small recurring link patterns, called motifs, appear more often than chance would suggest, much as common words recur in a language.

The authors catalogued motifs in brain maps from several species and compared them with random networks. Certain motifs stood out, hinting at design rules for how brains are wired. Motif counts give a compact way to compare healthy and disordered brains, or brains across species. The paper helped bring network math into neuroscience, where it now shapes how brain maps are read.
plos-pone-0000069:
Lester M. Shulman, Yossi Manor, Danit Sofer, and a large team searched sewage for poliovirus in PLOS ONE in 2006. In places where most people are vaccinated, the live polio vaccine itself can, on rare occasions, change back toward a harmful form. Those vaccine-derived viruses can pass through the gut and out into sewage.

Finding them in sewage is an early warning that they are circulating. The team reports such neurovirulent strains in a highly immune population, where few would expect them. Sewage testing thus acts as a silent sentinel for polio control. It can spot risk before any child falls ill, which is exactly what the endgame of polio eradication needs.
plos-pone-0000169:
Roderick Nigel Finn and Børge A. Kristoffersen published this evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Vitellogenin is the protein that stocks fish eggs with yolk. The authors examine how this gene was duplicated in vertebrates, testing the so-called 3R hypothesis of genome doublings. They link the copies to the floating pelagic egg and to the great spread of teleost fishes in the oceans.

Teleosts make up most fish species alive today, so their egg strategy matters at scale. The authors connect gene duplication timing to the rise of the buoyant ocean egg. The paper ties a DNA-level event to one of the biggest radiations in vertebrate history.
plos-pone-0000269:
Doris Estrugo, Alexander Fischer, Franziska Hess, and colleagues published this leukemia study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Integrins are the anchors cells use to grip their surroundings, and beta1 integrins sit on leukemia cells. The authors report that when these anchors are bound to their ligands, they inhibit procaspase-8, a starter protein of cell death. In doing so they mediate resistance to drugs and radiation that depends on cell adhesion.

Leukemia cells hiding in the bone marrow can survive chemotherapy by gripping their niche. This paper names the molecular brake that grip applies to the death machinery. Blocking that protective signal could make standard treatments work on cells that currently outlast them.
plos-pone-0000369:
Daryl Wile and Evan Balaban explored how the brain hears pitch, in a paper published in PLOS ONE in 2007. When people hear a musical note, they sense one whole pitch even when the sound is built from many parts. The authors looked for a brain signal that matches that whole-note sense of pitch.

Their study reports an auditory neural correlate, a pattern of brain activity that tracks pitch as a single quality rather than piece by piece. Work of this kind helps explain how the hearing system builds a simple sensation out of complex sound. It also bears on how people perceive music and speech, where pitch carries much of the meaning.
plos-pone-0000469:
Claude Sadis and colleagues found a protective side to nicotine in kidney injury, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The injury model is ischemia/reperfusion, where blood flow to the kidney stops and then returns, paradoxically causing extra damage through inflammation. The team showed nicotine protects the kidney from this injury through the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway.

That pathway is a nerve-based brake on inflammation, triggered through the same receptors nicotine acts on. The finding does not make smoking safe; it isolates one drug-like action worth copying without tobacco. Separating nicotine's anti-inflammatory effect from its harms is the kind of lead that can seed new medicines for transplant and shock patients.
plos-pone-0000569:
David Liska and colleagues compared how body fat is distributed among obese teenagers of different backgrounds, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The team measured interethnic differences in fat partitioning in obese adolescents. They looked at muscle, liver, and abdominal fat. Where fat is stored matters as much as how much there is.

Fat in the liver and deep abdomen drives diabetes and heart risk far more than fat under the skin. If ethnic groups partition fat differently at the same weight, risk screening by weight alone will misjudge many teens. Studies like this argue for measuring the dangerous depots directly in high-risk youth.
plos-pone-0000669:
Gilles Mirambeau, Sébastien Lyonnais, Dominique Coulaud and co-authors watched two HIV enzymes shape the virus's inner shell, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The HIV-1 nucleocapsid forms as the virus matures, a process directed by the viral protease. After infection, reverse transcriptase copies the viral genome, and the nucleocapsid transforms into pre-integration complexes in the cell's cytoplasm.

Using transmission electron microscopy in detail, the team examined the nucleocapsid's architecture. Their title states that protease and reverse transcriptase together control that structure. Both enzymes are already drug targets. Showing they also act as architects adds a new way to think about blocking the virus.
plos-pone-0000769:
Joern Kamradt, Volker Jung, Kerstin Wahrheit and colleagues scanned prostate cancer cell lines for newly amplified genome regions, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their purpose was to prove a longmer oligonucleotide microarray platform can profile gene copy number alterations. Amplicons are stretches of DNA copied many times in cancer cells. A genome-wide screen of such changes can quickly indicate novel candidate genes.

Candidates flagged this way may play a role in carcinogenesis, the making of cancer. Comprehensive profiling replaces one-gene-at-a-time searching with a single sweep. Each new amplicon is a lead: somewhere inside it may sit a gene whose extra copies drive tumor growth, and which drugs could target.
plos-pone-0000869:
Britta Eickholt, Aminul Ahmed, Meirion Davies and co-authors studied a single enzyme form called p110 delta in nerve growth, for PLOS ONE in 2007. The enzyme belongs to the PI 3-kinase family, which has eight forms whose roles in the nervous system were unclear. The p110 delta form was mostly known from white blood cells.

The team asked what this form does in sensory neurons, the cells that carry signals from skin and muscle. They focused on how axons, the long fibers of nerve cells, grow and regrow after damage. Knowing which enzyme form drives regrowth could guide later work on nerve repair.
plos-pone-0000969:
Eleonora Castelletti, Sergio Lo Caputo, Louise Kuhn and colleagues studied a mucosal signal chemical in HIV infection, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The chemical, CCL28 or MEC, draws antibody making cells into moist body linings. Those cells release IgA, the antibody that guards mucosal surfaces.

HIV specific IgA shows up both in infected people and in some exposed people who stay uninfected. The team analyzed the CCL28 circuit across infected, exposed and unexposed groups. Mucosal defense is where HIV usually enters, so its local signals matter. Work of this kind may help explain why a few exposed people resist infection.
plos-pone-0001069:
Sacha Genovesi, Liviana Leita, Paolo Sequi and colleagues directly detected prions bound in soil, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Scrapie in sheep and chronic wasting disease in deer are contagious prion diseases. Spread through the environment seems important in keeping these epidemics going, with contaminated ground as a reservoir.

Detecting prions in soil, rather than inferring them from sick animals, was the missing step. The team present a direct detection method for soil bound prions. Land where deer or sheep gather could then be tested before animals are moved there. Environmental control of prion disease depends on exactly this kind of tool.
plos-pone-0001169:
Building a brain means first making many progenitor cells, then having them stop dividing and become neurons. Barbara Hämmerle and Francisco Tejedor describe a new role for the Delta-Notch signaling system in that switch, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The transition from proliferation to neurogenesis is a crucial step in development.

The authors report a novel function of Delta-Notch signaling that mediates this transition in neural progenitor cells. A complete account of neurogenesis needs the molecular processes that govern each such step. Their finding adds a control point that other researchers can probe when development goes wrong.
plos-pone-0001269:
Hutchinson-Gilford progeria is a rare disorder of accelerated aging, caused in most cases by a specific mutation in the LMNA gene. Dayle McClintock and colleagues report that the mutant protein appears in ordinary aging skin too, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Progeria patients age fast and often die early, frequently from stroke or heart disease.

The authors show that the mutant form of lamin A acts as a biomarker of cellular aging in human skin, detectable beyond the disease itself. In other words, the progeria mechanism leaves traces in normal aging. That widens the relevance of studying this rare disease.
plos-pone-0001369:
Christopher Kanakry and co-authors published a 2007 PLOS ONE study on a growth factor called neuregulin-1. The gene for this factor has been linked to a higher risk of a severe mental illness. The same factor also plays a part in how the brain grows and how cancer spreads through the body.

Using blood cells grown in the lab, the team traced how the factor helps cells stick to each other. They found a chain of signals inside the cell that drives this effect. The findings tie one gene to both brain growth and cancer spread. That link may guide new work on both fields.
plos-pone-0001469:
Jun Cui and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE model of the switch that tells a cell to die. A family of proteins acts as a checkpoint for this death program, called apoptosis. How its parts interact was still in dispute. The team's past models had backed one account of the switch over others.

Here they show the switch holds two self boosting loops that can lock it in two states. Such a lock makes cell death a firm, one way choice once it flips. A clear model helps labs test drugs that flip the switch in cancer. It also explains why half measures tend to fail in this system.
plos-pone-0001569:
Yanjun Jiang, Dongsheng Xu, and Yong Zhao published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two cancer viruses in one tumor type. Both viruses, tied to Kaposi's sarcoma and to mono, belong to one virus family. Most cases of a rare AIDS linked lymphoma carry both. Each virus can wake and copy itself via a starter protein.

The team show the two starters hold each other back when both viruses share a cell. That mutual brake may keep both viruses quiet in the tumor. It is a neat case of rivals checking each other. It also shapes how drugs that wake one virus might act on the pair.
plos-pone-0001669:
Laurent Gillet, Susanna Colaco, and Philip G. Stevenson studied how a mouse herpesvirus first grabs hold of cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The first contact a virus makes largely decides which cells it can infect. Murid herpesvirus-4 depends heavily on glycosaminoglycans, long sugar chains on cell surfaces, for binding.

That dependence pointed to one of the virus's own surface glycoproteins as the sugar-binding part. The authors tested the gH and gL protein pair and report that this complex binds glycosaminoglycans. The full text gives the binding assays and the mutants they used to confirm the contact. A virus's first grip on a cell is a natural drug and vaccine target, since blocking it can stop infection before it starts.
plos-pone-0001769:
Sylvane Desrivières, Kristina Krause, Anne Dyer, and their co-authors linked a signaling gene to teenage drinking behavior in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The PI3K pathway usually regulates cell growth and survival. Growing evidence tied it to behavioral responses to addictive drugs, which made its genes candidates for addiction risk.

The team reports that sequence variation in the PI3K p85 alpha gene associates with alcohol risk drinking behavior in adolescents. The full text gives the teen sample and the variant statistics. A gene in a drug-response pathway showing up in teenage drinking supports the view that addiction risk is partly hard-wired. That could one day guide early prevention for high-risk youth.
plos-pone-0001869:
Hiroshi Ageta and co-authors published a brain study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on activin, a hormone that helps cells grow and change type. Activin was already known to shield brain cells from harm when blood flow fails. The team asked what else activin does inside the brain. They focused on mood, and on the growth of new brain cells in adult animals.

The authors report that activin in the brain shapes acts linked to fear and stress. It also shapes adult neurogenesis, the birth of new neurons in grown animals. Readers get a clear case that a growth hormone can sway both behavior and brain repair. That link matters for work on mood disorders and on how the adult brain renews itself.
plos-pone-0001969:
Michael Forbes and co-authors compared ear infection strains of a common bacterium in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The bacterium, Streptococcus pneumoniae, causes both local ills, such as ear infection, and body-wide disease. How much of that variety comes from the strain's genes, its serotype, or the host's response was not fully clear.

The team used a chinchilla model of otitis media, infection of the middle ear, to score each strain's virulence under the same host conditions. Holding the host fixed lets strain traits stand out. Such scores help predict which strains cause the worst disease, and which a vaccine must cover.
plos-pone-0002069:
Paloma Alonso-Magdalena and co-authors studied how estrogen shapes insulin stores in the pancreas, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Pancreatic beta cells make and release insulin, the main hormone that keeps blood sugar in balance. Estrogen receptors, in two forms called alpha and beta, play a part in glucose control, yet their role inside beta cells was still grey.

As the title states, the team report that the alpha form, ER alpha, regulates how much insulin the pancreas holds. A hormone better known for reproduction thus also tunes the insulin supply. That link may help explain sex gaps in diabetes risk.
plos-pone-0002169:
Omar Salim, Ian Clarke, and Paul Lambden examined the front end of the genome of a cattle virus, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Jena virus is a bovine norovirus that causes gut disease in cattle. It serves as a workable model for the noroviruses that infect the gut of people, which are hard to study directly.

The virus carries a single strand of RNA with sections that code first for building proteins, then for its shell. The team analyzed the 5 prime end of that genome to see how its parts are arranged and controlled. Details at this level guide work on how noroviruses copy themselves.
plos-pone-0002269:
Mahomed Patel and co-authors built a framework for judging how ready family doctors are for a flu pandemic. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Primary care, and general practice above all, will stand at the frontline when pandemic influenza hits. Yet no framework existed to guide systematic planning for that task or to compare the plans countries had drawn up.

The authors aimed to create such a framework and to test it against plans from five countries. A common yardstick lets health systems spot the gaps in their own plans before a crisis exposes them. General practice is where most patients will first turn.
plos-pone-0002369:
Liao and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Anne P. Liao, Elaine O. Petrof, Sumalatha Kuppireddi, among others. Its subject is salmonella Type III Effector AvrA Stabilizes Cell Tight Junctions to Inhibit Inflammation in Intestinal Epithelial Cells. Salmonella Typhimurium is a major cause of human gastroenteritis.

The Salmonella type III secretory system secretes virulence proteins, called effectors. Effectors are responsible for the change of tight junction (TJ) structure and function in intestinal epithelial cells. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002469:
Karkan, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Delara Karkan, Cheryl Pfeifer, Timothy Z. Vitalis, among others. Its subject is a Unique Carrier for Delivery of Therapeutic Compounds beyond the Blood-Brain Barrier.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002569:
Pérez-Mancera and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Pedro A. Pérez-Mancera, Camino Bermejo-Rodríguez, Manuel Sánchez-Martín, among others. Its subject is fUS-DDIT3 Prevents the Development of Adipocytic Precursors in Liposarcoma by Repressing PPARγ and C/EBPα and Activating eIF4E. FUS-DDIT3 is a chimeric protein generated by the most common chromosomal translocation t(12;16)(q13;p11) linked to liposarcomas.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002669:
In 2008, Joenna Driemeyer and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about changes in gray matter induced by Learning—Revisited. Authorship is credited in the record to Joenna Driemeyer and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Recently, activation-dependant structural brain plasticity in humans has been demonstrated in adults after three months of training a visio-motor skill. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002769:
Ulrich Meinzer and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of nod2 mediates susceptibility to yersinia pseudotuberculosis in mice. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Ulrich Meinzer, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Nucleotide oligomerisation domain 2 (NOD2) is a component of the innate immunity known to be involved in the homeostasis of Peyer patches (PPs) in. A further point appears in the abstract. However, little is known about its role during gut infection in vivo . Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002869:
Nasir Salam, Shashank Gupta, Sachin Sharma and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on protection against tuberculosis. Their focus was dendritic cells, a type of immune cell that helps start T cell responses. They asked how two signal proteins, RANTES and IP-10, shape that protection when cells are treated with the bacterial protein CFP-10.

The work looks at how treated dendritic cells prime T cells and guide immune responses to mycobacteria. It links chemokine and cytokine signals to the strength of the response. Readers get a lab-based view of one route the immune system may use to fight Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the germ that causes tuberculosis.
plos-pone-0002969:
Cathrin Bruederle, Robert Hnasko, Thomas Kraemer and co-authors tested whether prion-infected meat-and-bone meal stays infectious after biodiesel production in 2008. The BSE epidemic had collapsed markets for beef by-products such as meat-and-bone meal, a protein-rich feed supplement. Normal rendering did not remove all concern about prions.

A key question was whether turning the fat into biodiesel also destroys infectivity in the remains. The title gives the answer: the meal is still infectious afterward. Published in PLOS ONE, the finding sets a hard limit on one proposed safe use for risky material. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003069:
Jean-Marc Melgari, Patrizio Pasqualetti, Flavia Pauri and co-authors mapped upper limb muscles in motor cortex together in 2008. Past work with transcranial magnetic stimulation focused on the cortical representation of a limited group of muscles. No attempt had recorded hand, forearm, and arm at once to disentangle a functional topography.

Their concert metaphor means muscles mapped as an ensemble, not soloists. Published in PLOS ONE, a joint map shows how the primary motor cortex organizes coordinated limb control. That matters for stroke rehabilitation, where recovery is about combined actions, not single muscles. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003169:
Hugo Merchant, Wilbert Zarco, Ramon Bartolo and colleagues examine how timing tasks relate to each other in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They measured performance links among ten different tasks that involved judging time intervals below one second, using multidimensional analyses. Twenty human subjects carried out explicit timing tasks such as interval categorization.

The authors argue that the context of temporal processing shows up in the pattern of links between tasks. Readers learn that timing is not one single skill but a set of related abilities. That view matters for brain research on time, music, speech, and movement control.
plos-pone-0003269:
Petra Vetter, Brian Butterworth and Bahador Bahrami test a classic claim about counting small sets in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Traditionally, visual enumeration of a small number of items, from one to about four, called subitizing, has been thought of as a parallel, pre-attentive process distinct from serial counting of larger numbers. The team tested this hypothesis by modulating attentional load.

The title reports that attentional load affects numerosity estimation, as evidence against a pre-attentive subitizing mechanism. Readers see a neat textbook split challenged by experiment. How we judge number at a glance matters for models of basic cognition.
plos-pone-0007469: The growth signal IL-3 and a cancer-causing version of the Abl protein both reshape blood-cell development. This study shows they do it not by changing which genes are switched on, but by altering how long the resulting messages survive. Controlling message lifespan turns out to be a powerful lever on the myeloblast's identity — one that leukemia exploits.
plos-pone-0007569: Gene-building blocks got a two-way reporter. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Martin's team built Gemini, a reporter that works two ways at once. Standard biological parts need clean readouts. The two-way reporter was validated. The reporter feeds synthetic biology.
plos-pone-0007669: Drugs that block VEGF starve tumors of blood vessels, but they also reshape the immune landscape inside. This study compared different anti-VEGF blockers in mouse breast cancer and found cytokine levels tracked with immune-cell invasion. The results show these drugs do more than cut off blood supply.
plos-pone-0007769: HIV's Tat protein drives the virus's replication, so this study built a broken version — Nullbasic — that jams the machinery instead. The mutant potently blocked multiple steps of HIV-1 replication. A saboteur protein could become a new kind of antiviral.
plos-pone-0007869: The brain's immune cells keep T cells in check. This 2009 study found that microglia and microglia-like cells differentiated from dendritic cells inhibit CD4 T cell proliferation. The finding illuminates how the central nervous system maintains its immune privilege.
plos-pone-0007969: Genome-wide association studies keep finding small-effect variants that explain little disease risk. This study asked how many variants remain undiscovered and how large studies must be to find them. The statistical forecast sets expectations for the genomics era.
plos-pone-0008069: An empire's expansion rewrote desert diets. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Vinton and colleagues examined how Inka rule changed household diets in northern Chile's Atacama Desert. Ancient plant remains from homes tracked the dietary shift. The archaeobotanical record shows what conquest put on the table.
plos-pone-0008169: Millions of orphans live in institutions, but is family care better? This study compared the wellbeing of orphans aged 6–12 in institutional versus community care across five poor nations. The evidence informs a global policy debate.
plos-pone-0008269: A flipped chromosome chunk was mapped for its effects. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Bosch's team assessed the nucleotide, cytogenetic, and expression impact of the human 8p23.1 inversion. Pierre Boaistuau's Histoires prodigieuses was the great French book of wonders of its century. Edward Fenton Englished it in 1569 as Certaine Secrete Wonders of Nature. Elizabethan readers, hungry for marvels, got sea monsters and strange births in their own language at last.
